entry.title: CAP Agents UI5 Web UI
entry.content:
Introduction

SAP recently released the @cap-js/agents plugin, which turns a CAP service into an AI agent that speaks the A2A protocol. You annotate a service, you get an agent that can query your entities, call your actions and even pause to ask the user for approval. It is a lot of capability for one annotation.

What you don’t get is a user interface you can ship. The agent is an endpoint, so talking to it means writing JSON-RPC by hand and reading server-sent events in a terminal. That gets old quickly.

So I built a plugin for it. In this blog post, I’ll show you how to add a full SAPUI5 chat client to any CAP project with agents, by installing one npm package and changing nothing else.

Problem

Once you add @AGent to a service, @cap-js/agents mounts an A2A endpoint for it. A2A is to agents what OData is to your entities: a standard wire format, so any client can talk to any agent. That is great for integration, less great when you just want to see if your agent works.

Sending a message looks like this:

curl -X POST http://localhost:4004/a2a/support \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "jsonrpc": "2.0",
    "id": 1,
    "method": "message/send",
    "params": {
      "message": {
        "kind": "message",
        "role": "user",
        "messageId": "1",
        "parts": [{ "kind": "text", "text": "list the open tickets" }]
      }
    }
  }'

That works, but it is not something you demo to a business user. And streaming makes it worse, message/stream returns server-sent events which you now have to read as raw text in your terminal.

To be fair, @cap-js/agents does ship a small chat preview, you’ll find it per agent at /a2a/<agent>/preview/. It is genuinely handy while developing and it even renders markdown, which mine does not do yet.

But it is a preview and SAP positions it as one, the README introduces it with “for local development”. It is a single plain HTML page and not a UI5 app. The way it authenticates gives it away: the page reads the browser’s Authorization header and reuses that for its own calls. That works locally with basic auth, behind an approuter with XSUAA your browser holds a session cookie instead and there is no such header to pass on. So it is great for trying things out on your laptop, it is not what you put in front of an end-user on BTP.

What I wanted was simple:

  • A real UI5 app, so it fits next to everything else we build on BTP
  • Streaming replies, so you see the agent working instead of staring at a spinner
  • Approve and reject buttons when the agent asks for human approval
  • A picker when a project has more than one agent
  • The same thing working after deployment to BTP, without a separate HTML5 app to maintain

Solution

That’s what cap-agent-ui5-webui does. It is a CAP plugin, so there is exactly one step:

npm add cap-agent-ui5-webui

CAP picks it up through the cds-plugin.js convention and the chat client is served at http://localhost:4004/chat/index.html. It also adds itself to the “Web Applications” list on the CDS welcome page, so you can just click it.

The chat client answering a question about the sample’s tickets

My first design was more complicated. I had a separate dev server for the UI5 app, until it became clear that with TypeScript and the CAP UI5 plugin none of that was needed. Cutting it out made the plugin both smaller and easier to explain 🙂

Everything is open source, the plugin lives in these two places:

  • npm package: https://www.npmjs.com/package/cap-agent-ui5-webui
  • GitHub repository: https://github.com/lemaiwo/cap-agent-ui5-webui

And if you’d rather read a working project than a README, there is a second repository that consumes the plugin, with the local, hybrid and deployed setups all wired up: https://github.com/lemaiwo/cap-agent-ui5-webui-sample

That sample is the shortest answer to “how do I use this in my own project”, have a look at its package.json, srv/support-service.cds and mta.yaml and you have seen everything there is to it.

Setting up the agent

The plugin does not create agents, it only gives you a UI for the ones you have. For a service to become an agent you need two annotations:

using { sample as db } from '../db/schema';

@agent
@protocol: ['odata', 'agent']
service SupportService {
  entity Tickets as projection on db.Tickets;
  entity Customers as projection on db.Customers;

  @AGent.hitl
  action escalate(ticket : Integer, reason : String) returns String;
}

Both of them are needed and this is the one thing I’d really like you to take away from this post:

  • @AGent alone gives you a working agent, but OData is no longer served
  • @protocol alone mounts the A2A endpoint and even serves a valid agent card, but no handlers are registered, so every message fails at runtime with buildGraph handler ... undefined

How it works

The UI is a freestyle SAPUI5 app in TypeScript. It talks to the agent directly over A2A, there is no proxy or backend-for-frontend in between:

Endpoint

Served by

What it is

/chat/index.html

the plugin

the chat client itself

/chat/agents.json

the plugin

the list of agents found in your project

/a2a/<service>

@cap-js/agents

the A2A endpoint, JSON-RPC over POST

/a2a/<service>/.well-known/agent-card.json

@cap-js/agents

the agent card

agents.json is the only piece the plugin generates itself. On served it walks your services, picks the ones carrying @AGent and returns them:

[{ "name": "SupportService", "path": "/a2a/support", "description": "SupportService" }]

That is what fills the agent picker. Because it is generated at runtime there is nothing to configure, add a second @AGent service and it shows up by itself.

Human in the loop

@AGent.hitl on an action is where this gets interesting. Instead of executing the action, the agent pauses in A2A state input-required and waits. The chat shows Approve and Reject buttons, only after you approve does the action actually run.

Configuration

Zero config by default. Everything below is optional, under cds["cap-agent-ui5-webui"] in your package.json:

Setting

Default

What it does

mountPath

/chat

where the UI and agents.json are served

enabled

true

set to false to switch the plugin off in a profile

bootstrapUrl

SAPUI5 CDN

point it at your own SAPUI5 copy for air-gapped or CSP restricted hosts

serveUi

true

set to false when you deploy the UI to the HTML5 Application Repository

agents

all @AGent services

an allow-list of service names, in the order you want them offered

The boolean shorthand works too, "cap-agent-ui5-webui": false disables the plugin completely.

Running it on BTP

This works deployed as well and by default there is nothing extra to set up. The plugin serves the UI from your CAP service, so you don’t need an HTML5 Application Repository, a content deployer or an extra module in your mta.yaml. You do still need an approuter, but only for login, since CAP’s auth middleware can reject with 401 and cannot redirect a browser to the identity provider.

If you do want the UI in the HTML5 Application Repository, for example because you want it in SAP Build Work Zone, that is supported too:

npx cap-agent-ui5-webui html5 app/chat-ui/dist
  • html5: the command that packages the chat UI for the repository
  • app/chat-ui/dist: the folder it writes to, this is generated output so keep it out of git

This writes the prebuilt UI, an xs-app.json and a deployable zip into that folder and prints the approuter routes you need to add. Combine it with serveUi: false in your production profile and the CDS server stops serving the UI, it only keeps agents.json, which has to stay there because it is generated at runtime.

Conclusion

There is a complete sample project on GitHub with all three setups, local, hybrid against a real model on SAP AI Core and deployed to BTP: https://github.com/lemaiwo/cap-agent-ui5-webui-sample

Clone it and run:

npm install
npm run dev

Then open http://localhost:4004/chat/index.html and ask it to list the open tickets. 

@cap-js/agents does the hard part, it turns your CAP service into an agent with tools, streaming and a human approval step. What was missing was a UI you can actually deploy. One npm add now gives you that, in your own project, on your own session and with your own agents listed automatically.

The plugin is small. It serves a page and a JSON file, everything else is your CAP project.

You can find it on GitHub and npm:

  • Plugin on npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/cap-agent-ui5-webui
  • Plugin source on GitHub: https://github.com/lemaiwo/cap-agent-ui5-webui
  • Sample project showing how to consume it: https://github.com/lemaiwo/cap-agent-ui5-webui-sample
  • SAP’s agents plugin: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@cap-js/agents

Kr, Wouter

entry.title: Integrate a Pro-Code CAP A2A Agent with Joule
entry.content:
Overview

 

In my previous blog Build a Pro-Code A2A Agent for SAP S/4HANA Cloud with the CAP Agent Plugin (Node.js), we deployed a pro-code CAP agent to SAP Cloud Foundry. This article shows how to surface that agent inside Joule — SAP’s AI copilot — which is integrated with SAP Work Zone.

 

Prerequisites
  • Unified Joule is set up and integrated with SAP Work Zone.
  • Joule Studio CLI is installed and authenticated.
  • SAP Cloud Foundry CLI is installed.

 

Procedure

 

Step 1 — Create a BTP Destination for the CAP A2A Agent

 

In your BTP sub-account, create a destination that points to the deployed pro-code CAP A2A Agent service URL.

 

Step 2 — Build the Joule Pro-Code Capability

 

Create a joule-capability/ folder in your project with the following files.

 

joule-capability/functions/call_agent.yaml
parameters:
  - name: contextId
    optional: true
  - name: taskId
    optional: true

action_groups:
  - actions:
      - type: status-update
        message: <? "Processing your delivery request..." ?>

      - type: agent-request
        agent_type: remote
        system_alias: OutboundDeliveryAgent
        body: >
          <? (contextId == null || contextId.isEmpty()) && (taskId == null || taskId.isEmpty())
             ? null
             : '{ "contextId": "' + contextId + '", "taskId": "' + taskId + '" }' ?>
        result_variable: result

      - type: set-variables
        variables:
          - name: contextId
            value: <? result.body.contextId ?>
          - name: taskId
            value: <? result.body.id ?>

      - type: message
        message:
          type: text
          content: "<? result.body.status.message.parts[0].text ?>"
          markdown: true

result:
  contextId: "<? contextId ?>"
  taskId: "<? taskId ?>"

 

joule-capability/scenarios/invoke_agent.yaml
description: >
  Invoke this agent for anything related to SAP S/4HANA outbound deliveries.
  Call this when the user asks to look up delivery documents, check delivery
  items, create a new outbound delivery, or query the status of a shipment.
  Examples: "Show me the outbound deliveries for shipping point 1000",
  "What items are in delivery 80000012?",
  "Create a delivery from sales order 5000001",
  "List all deliveries for this week".

target:
  type: function
  name: call_agent
  parameters:
    - name: contextId
      value: $capability_context.contextId
    - name: taskId
      value: $capability_context.taskId

capability_context:
  - name: contextId
    value: $target_result.contextId
  - name: taskId
    value: $target_result.taskId

 

joule-capability/capability_context.yaml
variables:
  - name: contextId
  - name: taskId

 

joule-capability/capability.sapdas.yaml
schema_version: 3.28.0

metadata:
  namespace: joule.ext
  name: capagents4_a2a
  version: 1.0.0
  display_name: "Outbound Delivery Agent"
  description: An A2A agent for managing SAP S/4HANA outbound deliveries. Handles querying delivery documents, delivery items, and creating new outbound deliveries.

system_aliases:
  OutboundDeliveryAgent:
    destination: capa2as4

 

joule-capability/da.sapdas.yaml
schema_version: 1.4.0
name: capagents4_a2a
capabilities:
  - type: local
    folder: ./

 

Step 3 — Deploy the Joule Capability

 

Log in with the Joule CLI and deploy the capability:
joule login --apiurl "<joule url>" -a "<ias url>" -c "<client id>" -s "<client secret>" --username "<user name>" --store-password --no-app-tid

joule deploy -c joule-capability/da.sapdas.yaml

 

 

 

Step 4 — Test the Deployed Capability

 

List deployed capabilities and launch a local test session:
joule list

joule launch

 

 

 

 

Step 5 — Integrate the Capability with Unified Joule in SAP Work Zone

 

Update the SAP Digital Assistant with the new capability:
joule update "sap_digital_assistant" --capability-file joule-capability/capability.sapdas.yaml

 

Step 6 — Test the Agent in SAP Work Zone

 

Open Joule in SAP Work Zone and interact with the outbound delivery agent.

 

 

 

The End! Thanks for your time! Jacky Liu

entry.title: Deploying SAPUI5 Apps to SAP Build Work Zone
entry.content:
Introduction

While working with SAPUI5 applications, I wanted to understand how an application developed in SAP Business Application Studio could be made available to users through SAP Build Work Zone. Creating and running the application locally was straightforward, but the deployment and Work Zone configuration involved a few additional steps.

I went through the complete process of creating a simple SAPUI5 application, configuring it for deployment to Cloud Foundry, and then making the deployed application available in SAP Build Work Zone. One thing I found useful was understanding how the application moves from BAS to Cloud Foundry and then becomes available through Work Zone's Content Explorer.

During the setup, I also noticed that successfully deploying the application to Cloud Foundry was only one part of the process. Work Zone needed to be refreshed before the deployed HTML5 application became available for import. This was one of the practical details that helped me understand how the different parts of the setup are connected.

In this blog, I'll walk through the approach step by step. By the end, you'll have a SAPUI5 application deployed to Cloud Foundry and available as a tile inside a SAP Build Work Zone site.

Step 1: Subscribe to SAP Build Work Zone

First, we need access to SAP Build Work Zone.

Open the SAP BTP Cockpit and navigate to:

Service Marketplace → SAP Build Work Zone, standard edition → Standard Subscription

Subscribe to the service.

This screenshot shows the SAP Build Work Zone, standard edition subscription option in the SAP BTP Service Marketplace.

The subscription gives us access to the Work Zone capabilities that we will use later to create a site and make our deployed application available to users.

Step 2: Assign the Launchpad Admin Role

After subscribing, we need the required permissions to manage Work Zone.

Go to:

Security → Users

Select your user and choose:

Assign Role Collection → Launchpad_Admin

Assign the role collection to your user.

After assigning the role, log out and log in again so that the updated permissions are applied.

This screenshot shows the Launchpad_Admin role collection being assigned to the user.

One small thing I noticed during the setup was that assigning the Launchpad_Admin role collection did not immediately reflect in my current session. I had to log out and log in again before the updated permissions were available.

This was useful to know because, without refreshing the session, it can look like the role assignment has not been applied correctly.

Step 3: Create a Site

Now open SAP Build Work Zone and go to:

Site Directory → Create Site

Give the site a suitable name and create it.

This screenshot shows the Site Directory where a new Work Zone site is created. The site will later contain the tile for our deployed SAPUI5 application.

At this point, we have the basic Work Zone setup ready. Next, we can create the SAPUI5 application that we want to deploy.

Step 4: Create a SAPUI5 Project

Now let's create the application that will eventually be deployed to Work Zone.

Open SAP Business Application Studio (BAS) and create a new project using:

New Project from Template → SAP Fiori Application → Basic App

For this example, I used a basic SAPUI5 application. The application is only used to demonstrate the deployment and Work Zone integration, but the same process can be followed for a real SAPUI5 or Fiori application.

Step 5: Enable Deployment Configuration

While creating the application, enable the deployment-related options:

  • Add deployment configuration
  • Add FLP configuration

These configurations are important because we are not only going to run the application locally. We also need the project to contain the configuration required for deployment and launchpad integration.

At this stage, BAS will add the required deployment and FLP-related configuration to the project.

Step 6: Select Cloud Foundry as the Deployment Target

For the deployment target, select:

Cloud Foundry

The application will be packaged and deployed to the Cloud Foundry environment in SAP BTP.

Make sure you have access to the required Cloud Foundry organization and space before starting the deployment.

Step 7: Configure the FLP Settings

Next, configure the launchpad-related information.

Provide values for:

  • Semantic Object
  • Action
  • Tile Title

For example:

Semantic Object: Employee
Action: display
Tile Title: Employee Application

These values are used when the application is exposed through the launchpad environment.

The exact values can be different depending on your application and navigation requirements.

Step 8: Run the Application Locally

Before deploying the application, I recommend checking that everything works locally.

Use the Preview Application option in BAS and verify that the application opens correctly.

For this example, you should see the basic application output, such as the Hello World screen.

This is a useful checkpoint because it allows us to make sure the application itself is working before moving on to the deployment steps.

Step 9: Build the MTA Project

Once the application is working, we need to create the deployment package.

In BAS, right-click:

mta.yaml → Build MTA Project

This generates the MTAR file that will be used for deployment to Cloud Foundry.

This screenshot shows the MTA project being built from mta.yaml. The generated MTAR package will be used for the Cloud Foundry deployment.

Step 10: Deploy to Cloud Foundry

After building the MTAR, deploy it to Cloud Foundry.

Start the deployment and log in when prompted.

During the deployment, make sure you select the correct:

  • Cloud Foundry Organization
  • Space

The MTAR package will then be deployed to the selected Cloud Foundry environment.

This screenshot shows the SAPUI5 application being deployed to the selected Cloud Foundry environment.

After deployment, I verified that the application was available under HTML5 Applications before moving on to the Work Zone configuration. This gave me a useful checkpoint to confirm that the Cloud Foundry deployment was completed successfully.

Step 11: Verify the Deployment

After the deployment is completed, open the SAP BTP Cockpit and check the HTML5 Applications section.

You should be able to find the deployed SAPUI5 application there.

This is an important checkpoint because it confirms that the application has been successfully deployed before we start configuring it in Work Zone.

Step 12: Refresh the HTML5 Applications in Work Zone

Now go back to SAP Build Work Zone.

Open:

Channel Manager

and refresh the HTML5 applications.

This allows Work Zone to detect the application that was recently deployed to Cloud Foundry.

This screenshot shows the Channel Manager being refreshed so that the newly deployed HTML5 application becomes available in Work Zone.

One thing that became clear to me during the process was that deploying the application to Cloud Foundry is not enough for it to immediately appear in Work Zone's Content Explorer.

This was the step that initially made the relationship between Cloud Foundry and Work Zone clearer to me.

After the deployment, I had to go to Channel Manager and refresh the HTML5 Applications content. Only after Work Zone refreshed the available applications could I continue to Content Explorer and add the deployed application.

This helped me understand the separation between the Cloud Foundry deployment and the Work Zone content configuration. The application can be successfully deployed, but Work Zone still needs to detect that newly deployed application before it can be added to the site.

Step 13: Import the Application

Next, go to:

Content Manager → Content Explorer → HTML5 Apps

Find your application and select Add.

This imports the deployed application into the Work Zone content environment.

This screenshot shows the deployed application available under HTML5 Apps in Content Explorer. The application is selected to add it to the Work Zone content.

At this point, I could see the application that had been deployed earlier in BAS and Cloud Foundry. This helped confirm that the application had successfully moved from the deployment environment into the Work Zone content environment.

Step 14: Create a Group

Now create a group for the application.

Go to:

Content Manager → Create → Group

Enable the Assignment Status option and save the group.

For example:

Group Name:
My Applications

This screenshot shows the creation of a Work Zone group that will be used to organize the application content.

Step 15: Assign the Application to the Everyone Role

Next, open:

Content Manager → Everyone Role

Assign the application to this role and save the changes.

This screenshot shows the SAPUI5 application being assigned to the Everyone role so that it can be made available to users accessing the site.

One thing I learned here was that importing an application into Work Zone is not the same as making it available to users. The application also needs to be assigned to the appropriate role and included in the site's content. This was an important distinction for me when I was going through the setup for the first time.

Step 16: Verify the Application in the Site

Finally, open the Work Zone site that you created earlier.

You should now see the application tile.

Click the tile and verify that the SAPUI5 application opens correctly.

This screenshot shows the SAPUI5 application displayed as a tile in the SAP Build Work Zone site. Selecting the tile launches the deployed application.

Key Learnings

During this implementation, a few things became clearer to me:

1. Role changes may require a new session

After assigning the Launchpad_Admin role collection, logging out and logging in again ensured that the updated permissions were available.

2. Cloud Foundry deployment and Work Zone configuration are separate steps

A successful Cloud Foundry deployment does not automatically mean that the application is immediately available in the Work Zone content environment. Checking the HTML5 Applications section first provides a useful checkpoint.

3. Refreshing Channel Manager is an important step

After deploying the application, refreshing the HTML5 Applications in Channel Manager allowed Work Zone to detect the newly deployed application. This helped me understand why an application that is already deployed may not immediately appear in Content Explorer.

Conclusion

When I first worked through this setup, the process looked like several independent configuration steps. After completing it, the overall flow became much clearer to me.

The most useful thing I learned was that deploying a SAPUI5 application to Cloud Foundry is only one part of making it available through SAP Build Work Zone. The application still needs to be detected by Work Zone, imported through Content Explorer, assigned to the appropriate role, and made available through a site.

Two small details were particularly useful during my setup: logging in again after assigning the Launchpad_Admin role collection and refreshing the HTML5 applications in Channel Manager after deployment. These helped me understand why newly assigned permissions or newly deployed applications may not be immediately reflected in the existing Work Zone session.

The overall flow became clear to me as:

BAS → Cloud Foundry → HTML5 Applications → Channel Manager → Content Explorer → Role/Group → Work Zone Site

Once this flow is understood, the same approach can be applied to other SAPUI5 applications that need to be made available through SAP Build Work Zone.

entry.title: SAP UI Integration Cards: Choosing the Right Development Path for Supplier Portals
entry.content:
Supplier Portal projects keep finding their way onto my calendar. Across industries, such as manufacturing, retail, energy, public sector, the pattern repeats: a company runs SAP in the back office, has hundreds or thousands of external suppliers, and needs to give those suppliers a meaningful digital touchpoint without onboarding them into the core system. SAP BTP, and specifically SAP Build Work Zone, is increasingly the answer. If I had to pick a top-5 use case for BTP, this is on the list and the reason is almost always the same: you need to give people outside your company controlled, identity-aware access to your processes. That is a non-trivial problem, and BTP is well-positioned to solve it cleanly.

What I also enjoy about this topic is how many technology layers it touches at once. Identity and access management, OData APIs, low-code tooling, process automation, UI frameworks, a Supplier Portal brings them all into play. It is one of those projects where a good architect genuinely has to think across the stack.

I am also speaking at the SAP Exploration Workshop: Supplier Portal later this year, so this has been on my mind a lot recently. This post grew out of preparation for that event,  specifically the question of how to explain UI Integration Cards to developers and architects who are new to the topic but need to make real implementation decisions fast.

The question teams consistently hit early is not what cards are, but which development path to take and when. There are two fundamentally different approaches:

  • Low-code (declarative): Everything lives in manifest.json. No JavaScript controller, no XML view, no build step. The framework handles rendering, theming, accessibility, and responsiveness. This covers eight of the nine card types and the vast majority of supplier portal use cases.
  • Pro-code (Component card): A full SAPUI5 component embedded in a card frame. Maximum flexibility, but you give up automatic theming, the Admin Console configuration panel, and declarative data binding and you take on full responsibility for Fiori compliance and the code maintenance.

Choosing the wrong path creates rework. This post maps both paths with supplier portal context throughout, then gives you a decision framework and highlights the manifest.json patterns, especially Work Zone context bindings and conditional expressions, that are rarely documented in one place.

All code examples are grounded in the official SAP UI5 Card Explorer.

The manifest.json Skeleton — Quick Anatomy

Every card, regardless of type or complexity, uses the same three-namespace structure: sap.app (card identity and metadata), sap.ui (UI5 technology declaration), and sap.card (type and content). The non-negotiable rules: sap.app/type must be "card" (not "application"), sap.app/id must be globally unique across your BTP tenant (use reverse-domain notation), and sap.card/type is the only always-required property within sap.card. For the full schema reference, see the Card Manifest Reference.

{
  "_version": "1.15.0",
  "sap.app": {
    "id": "com.company.supplier.cards.my-card",
    "type": "card",
    "applicationVersion": { "version": "1.0.0" }
  },
  "sap.ui": { "technology": "UI5" },
  "sap.card": { "type": "List" }
}

Everything else, such as header, data source, content layout, parameters, destinations is added inside sap.card.

Card Types at a Glance

Eight types are declarative (low-code). One (Component) is the pro-code escape hatch. For the full type documentation and live examples, browse the SAP UI5 Card Explorer directly.

Type Available In Best For

ListSAPUI5 + OpenUI5Orders, alerts, notifications, item feeds
TableSAPUI5 + OpenUI5Inventory tables, reports, structured comparisons
ObjectSAPUI5 + OpenUI5Supplier profiles, order details, record mastercards
TimelineSAPUI5 onlyOnboarding milestones, approval histories, activity logs
AnalyticalSAPUI5 onlyKPI tiles, spend dashboards, bar/donut/line charts
CalendarSAPUI5 + OpenUI5Appointment scheduling, event streams
AdaptiveCardSAPUI5 + OpenUI5Microsoft Adaptive Cards spec content
WebPageSAPUI5 + OpenUI5Embedded web page / iFrame
ComponentSAPUI5 + OpenUI5Full SAPUI5 component — pro-code only

Supplier Portal Use Cases - Card Type Mapping

Before choosing a card type, map your use case to the right type. The table below covers the most common supplier portal scenarios:

Supplier Portal Use Case Card Type Typical Data Source Key manifest.json Pattern

Open purchase orders feedListConditional highlight expression on order amount
Delivery alerts & quality notificationsListhighlight: Error/Warning/Success driven by status field
Invoice status overviewTableOne column per field; "identifier": true on invoice ID
Supplier master data / company profileObjectWork Zone context binding for auto-personalization
Spend KPIs & budget consumptionAnalyticalNumeric header + StackedColumn chart
Delivery performance trendAnalyticalLine or bar chart with trend indicator in header
Onboarding milestone trackerTimelinePer-item icon expression on task status field
Approval history logTimelineChronological task events with dateTime binding
Upcoming supplier calls & meetingsCalendarAppointment template with start/end ISO binding
Custom multi-tab scorecard or map viewComponentFull SAPUI5 component — pro-code path required

Path 1 — Low-Code: Manifest-Only Development

The low-code path covers all eight declarative types. You configure everything, such as data source, layout, interactions inside manifest.json. The framework handles rendering, theming, accessibility, and responsiveness.

For full manifest examples and interactive live previews of each type, the SAP UI5 Card Explorer is the authoritative reference. The four supplier portal scenarios below call out the manifest.json patterns worth understanding before you start: things the documentation covers individually but rarely connects together.

List Card - Open Orders & Alerts

→ Card Explorer: List Card

The List Card is the workhorse for feed-style data: open purchase orders, delivery alerts, quality notifications. Two patterns to know:

  • Binding expressions on highlight, icon, and info fields drive conditional UX entirely declaratively, no controller needed. Syntax: {= ${Amount} > 100000 ? 'Warning' : 'Success'}. The {= ... } expression form works anywhere a string value is expected in the manifest.
  • Configurable parameters ({{parameters.maxItems}}) let portal admins adjust list length in the Admin Console without touching the manifest, making the same card reusable across multiple portal pages with different display needs. Always add withCredentials: true to data.request so the app router forwards the user's Work Zone session to the backend.

Object Card - Supplier Profile

→ Card Explorer: Object Card · Object Card in Focus - SAP Community, Jul 2026

The Object Card renders a single business record as grouped label/value pairs. It is the natural fit for a supplier's master data view. The key pattern: wire a parameter like supplierId to {context>sap.workzone/currentUser/id/value} (see the Work Zone Context Bindings section below) so the card auto-loads the current user's profile on every page load without any server-side identity resolution logic.

Analytical Card - KPI Dashboard & Spend Charts

→ Card Explorer: Analytical Card

The Analytical Card pairs a "type": "Numeric" header, such as KPI figure, unit, trend indicator, and up to two side indicators with a chart body (StackedColumn, bar, Donut, Line). Use it for spend dashboards, delivery performance KPIs, or quality rate trends on the supplier homepage. Start with inline data.json for a static prototype, then swap in a data.request block to pull from a live OData or REST endpoint. Requires full SAPUI5.

Timeline Card - Onboarding Progress

→ Card Explorer: Timeline Card

The Timeline Card renders ordered, time-stamped events. It is the right choice for supplier onboarding milestone trackers or approval histories. Combine with a {{parameters.currentUser}} context binding (see below) to scope the timeline to the logged-in supplier's workflow instances. Binding expressions work on icon.src too: {= ${status} === 'COMPLETED' ? 'sap-icon://accept' : 'sap-icon://pending'} drives per-item icons dynamically with no controller.

Connecting Cards to SAP BTP Destinations

When a card runs inside SAP Build Work Zone, all backend calls are proxied through the application router. You cannot use absolute backend URLs, but you must declare named destinations and reference them as {{destinations.myDestination}}.

The BTP destination (BTP Cockpit → Connectivity → Destinations) must include these additional properties:

Property Required Value Why

HTML5.DynamicDestinationtrueMandatory. Allows the app router to resolve the destination dynamically at runtime. Without it, card requests return 404 or fail silently.
WebIDEEnabledtrueRequired for SAP Business Application Studio tooling to detect the destination.
WebIDEUsageodata_genUse odata_abap for ABAP systems; SuccessFactorsExtensionCard for SuccessFactors.

Declare the destination in the manifest under configuration.destinations:

{
  "sap.card": {
    "configuration": {
      "destinations": {
        "s4hana": {
          "name": "MY_S4H_DESTINATION",
          "defaultUrl": "/sap/opu/odata/sap/",
          "label": "S/4HANA Backend"
        }
      }
    },
    "data": {
      "request": {
        "url": "{{destinations.s4hana}}/sap/opu/odata/sap/API_BUSINESS_PARTNER/A_BusinessPartner",
        "parameters": { "$format": "json", "$top": "10" },
        "withCredentials": true
      },
      "path": "/d/results"
    }
  }
}

The name property maps the manifest's logical alias (s4hana) to the physical BTP destination name. This indirection means you can change the target system without editing the manifest. This is very useful when promoting cards across landscapes.

Work Zone Context Bindings 

This is one of the most practically useful patterns in the card framework, and one of the least documented in one place. Work Zone injects a set of context variables at runtime that you can bind directly to card parameters to enable personalized, identity-aware cards with zero server-side user resolution logic.

Here is an example using the Context Bindings as a data. 

"configuration": {
  "parameters": {
    "currentUserId": {
      "value": "{context>sap.workzone/currentUser/id/value}",
      "type": "string",
      "visible": false
    },
    "tenantHost": {
      "value": "{context>sap.workzone/currentCompany/webHost/value}",
      "type": "string",
      "visible": false
    },
    "sfUserId": {
      "value": "{context>sap.successfactors/currentUser/id/value}",
      "type": "string",
      "visible": false
    }
  }
}

Once declared, reference them anywhere in the manifest with {{parameters.currentUserId}} — including inside data.request.url, $filter query parameters, or request headers.

Complete Context Variable Reference

Context Variable Description Availability

{context>sap.workzone/currentUser/id/value}Logged-in user's UUID in Work ZoneWZ Standard & Advanced
{context>sap.workzone/currentUser/name/value}Logged-in user's display nameWZ Standard & Advanced
{context>sap.workzone/currentUser/email/value}Logged-in user's email addressWZ Standard & Advanced
{context>sap.workzone/currentUser/firstName/value}User's first nameWZ Standard & Advanced
{context>sap.workzone/currentUser/lastName/value}User's last nameWZ Standard & Advanced
{context>sap.workzone/currentCompany/id/value}Work Zone company/tenant IDWZ Standard & Advanced
{context>sap.workzone/currentCompany/webHost/value}Tenant web host (for constructing URLs)WZ Standard & Advanced
{context>sap.successfactors/currentUser/id/value}SAP SuccessFactors user IDSuccessFactors Work Zone
{context>sap.successfactors/currentUser/name/value}SAP SuccessFactors display nameSuccessFactors Work Zone

Practical use cases for supplier portals:

  • Personalized data fetch: use currentUser/id to filter an OData query to the current supplier's records.
  • Dynamic URL construction: use currentCompany/webHost to build tenant-specific deep links in navigation actions.
  • SuccessFactors cross-scenario: if your supplier portal also hosts HR self-service cards, sap.successfactors/currentUser/id lets you target SF OData endpoints without a separate identity resolution call.

Path 2 — Pro-Code: Component Cards

The Component card type loads a full SAPUI5 component. Essentially it is a mini-application embedded in a card frame. Choose this path only when:

  • Your layout cannot be expressed by any of the eight declarative types (e.g., a custom multi-tab view, a map widget, a D3 chart).
  • You need complex client-side business logic (multi-step form validation, dynamic data dependencies between fields).
  • You are wrapping an existing SAPUI5 application fragment as a card.

The manifest for a Component card delegates rendering to SAPUI5:

{
  "_version": "1.15.0",
  "sap.app": {
    "id": "com.company.supplier.cards.custom-scorecard",
    "type": "card",
    "applicationVersion": { "version": "1.0.0" }
  },
  "sap.card": {
    "type": "Component",
    "header": {
      "title": "Supplier Scorecard",
      "subTitle": "Custom performance view"
    }
  },
  "sap.ui5": {
    "rootView": {
      "viewName": "com.company.supplier.cards.custom-scorecard.view.Main",
      "type": "XML",
      "async": true
    },
    "dependencies": {
      "minUI5Version": "1.90.0",
      "libs": {
        "sap.ui.core":   {},
        "sap.m":         {},
        "sap.ui.layout": {}
      }
    }
  }
}

The corresponding project structure adds a full SAPUI5 component alongside the manifest:

my-component-card/
├── manifest.json
├── Component.js            ← SAPUI5 UIComponent
├── view/
│   └── Main.view.xml       ← XML view
├── controller/
│   └── Main.controller.js
└── i18n/
    └── i18n.properties

The architectural cost to factor in: Component cards require you to manually implement SAP Fiori design guidelines. The automatic theming, accessibility guarantees, and Admin Console configuration panel that declarative cards provide for free become your responsibility. This also means that when SAP updates Work Zone's design system or theming tokens, your Component card will not automatically pick up the changes. 

Decision Framework: Which Path Should You Choose?

Use these questions to reach the right decision before writing any code:

Question If YES → Recommendation

Does your data fit a list, table, object, chart, or timeline pattern?Low-CodeUse the corresponding declarative type
Do you need the card to be configurable by portal admins (no code)?Low-CodeUse configuration.parameters
Is the card connecting to a single BTP destination OData/REST endpoint?Low-CodeDeclarative data.request handles this
Do you need per-user personalization?Low-CodeUse Work Zone context bindings
Does your layout require multiple tabs, a wizard, or a custom chart library?Pro-CodeUse Component card
Do you need complex client-side validation or multi-step logic?Pro-CodeUse Component card
Will non-developers maintain or reconfigure the card post-deployment?Low-CodeDeclarative cards have a built-in admin UI
Are you wrapping an existing SAPUI5 app fragment?Pro-CodeComponent card is the right vessel

If the answer to most questions points to Low-Code but one layout requirement pushes toward Pro-Code, reconsider the layout requirement first. A different declarative type or a grouped Object card often solves what initially seems to need a custom component.

Project Structure and Tooling

A complete low-code card project in SAP Business Application Studio:

my-card-project/
├── manifest.json             ← Card definition (only required file)
├── i18n/
│   ├── i18n.properties       ← Default translations
│   └── i18n_de.properties    ← German translations
├── dt/
│   └── configuration.js      ← Design-time editor 
└── data/
    └── sample-data.json      ← Static data for BAS preview

Reference i18n keys anywhere in the manifest with double-brace syntax (same as parameters):

{
  "sap.app": {
    "id": "com.company.cards.orders",
    "type": "card",
    "i18n": "i18n/i18n.properties"
  },
  "sap.card": {
    "header": {
      "title": "{{CARD_TITLE}}",
      "subTitle": "{{CARD_SUBTITLE}}"
    }
  }
}
# i18n/i18n.properties
CARD_TITLE=Open Purchase Orders
CARD_SUBTITLE=Requires your attention

Summary

The key takeaways for architects designing content on SAP Build Work Zone for supplier portal scenarios:

  • Default to declarative. List, Table, Object, Analytical, and Timeline cards cover the standard supplier portal scenarios. The framework's rendering, theming, and Admin Console integration are worth preserving.
  • Use Work Zone context bindings ({context>sap.workzone/currentUser/id/value}) to build personalized, identity-aware cards without server-side user resolution logic. This pattern is underused and more powerful than it looks.
  • Use binding expressions ({= ${field} > threshold ? 'Warning' : 'Success'}) for conditional UX — colours, icons, labels — without needing a controller.
  • Get the BTP destination right first. HTML5.DynamicDestination: true is not optional, and the July 2025 alias change in Standard Edition catches teams that haven't updated.
  • Reserve Component for genuine outliers — complex layouts or logic that the declarative model cannot express — and factor in the Admin Console governance cost before committing.

The full reference for all card types, manifest properties, and live examples is available in the SAP UI5 Card Explorer.

entry.title: SAP BTP Work Zone - Authentication and Authorization, with On prem system
entry.content:
Recently I was working on deploying apps from SAP BTP and an on-premise SAP S/4HANA system to SAP Build Work Zone. The most important question from stakeholders was: how does access actually work when the app itself lives in S/4HANA? This post answers that question first with a simple example, and then walks through the configuration I used to make it work.

To make it easy to understand, imagine you run an enterprise called Central Inc. You want every employee to have one single launchpad to access apps from different systems: S/4HANA (Finance), SuccessFactors (HR) and Ariba (Procurement). That central launchpad is SAP Build Work Zone.

The Scene: Two Keys Needed for Every User

Our user, Maria, works in Procurement. To do her job, she needs access to the Create Purchase Order app.

This app lives inside the S/4HANA system, but we want her to launch it from Work Zone. This requires two distinct keys working together.

Key 1: The UI Key (Federated BTP Role Collection)

Work Zone uses content federation. It imports the S/4HANA UI content (business roles, spaces, pages and tiles) into Work Zone, so nothing has to be rebuilt manually in the cloud.

For every federated business role, a BTP role collection is generated automatically, named after the content provider ID and the backend role, e.g. ~s4h_SAP_BR_PURCHASER.

What this key does: When Maria logs in to Work Zone, her identity (via SAP Cloud Identity Services / Microsoft Entra ID) is mapped to this role collection. This lets her see and click the Purchase Order tile on her homepage. This key only gets her into the lobby of the building.

Key 2: The Data Key (Backend PFCG Role)

Maria clicks the tile. The app is now running and needs to read and write live data in S/4HANA.

Principal propagation through the SAP Cloud Connector securely passes Maria's identity down to S/4HANA. S/4HANA maps it to her local user (SU01) and checks: does Maria have the PFCG role SAP_BR_PURCHASER (and its authorizations) in this system?

What this key does: If the role is assigned, she is authorized to work with the specific business data. This key opens the locked office door and gives access to the actual files.

Configuration Walkthrough

Below are the steps I followed to set this up end to end. Names such as s4h and S4H_RT are examples; use your own naming conventions.

Step 1: Expose the business roles in S/4HANA

  1. Make sure the business roles you want to federate (e.g. SAP_BR_PURCHASER) have their launchpad spaces and pages assigned.
  2. Open transaction /UI2/CDM3_EXP_SCOPE, select the roles and choose Expose.
  3. Repeat the exposure whenever the roles, spaces or pages change, so Work Zone can pick up the updates.

Step 2: Connect S/4HANA through the Cloud Connector

  1. In the Cloud Connector, add a Cloud to On-Premise mapping to your S/4HANA system (protocol HTTPS, virtual host and port).
  2. Set Principal Type to X.509 Certificate so that principal propagation is possible.
  3. Expose the required resource paths, typically /sap/bc/ui2/cdm3/, /sap/opu/odata/, /sap/opu/odata4/, /sap/bc/ui5_ui5/ and /sap/public/bc/.
  4. Under Configuration > On Premise, create the system certificate and the CA certificate for principal propagation, and synchronize trust with your subaccount.

Step 3: Trust the Cloud Connector in S/4HANA

  1. Import the Cloud Connector CA/system certificate into the SSL server PSE in STRUST.
  2. Set the ICM profile parameters icm/HTTPS/trust_client_with_issuer and icm/HTTPS/trust_client_with_subject to the issuer and subject of the Cloud Connector system certificate, then restart the ICM.
  3. In CERTRULE, create a rule that maps the short-lived user certificate (e.g. the CN or e-mail) to the SU01 user. This is where Maria's cloud identity becomes her backend user.

Step 4: Create the destinations in the BTP subaccount

  • Design-time destination (e.g. S4H_DT😞 URL http://<virtual-host>:<port>/sap/bc/ui2/cdm3/entities, Proxy Type OnPremise, authentication with a technical user (or principal propagation), plus the property sap-client. Work Zone uses it to fetch the exposed content.
  • Runtime destination (e.g. S4H_RT😞 URL http://<virtual-host>:<port>, Proxy Type OnPremise, Authentication PrincipalPropagation, plus sap-client and HTML5.DynamicDestination = true. Apps use it when Maria opens them. Point the runtime destination for OData to the same destination unless your landscape separates them.

Step 5: Add S/4HANA as a content provider in Work Zone

  1. In the Site Manager, open the Channel Manager and choose New > Content Provider.
  2. Enter a title and an ID (e.g. s4h; this becomes the prefix of the generated role collections), and select the design-time and runtime destinations.
  3. Choose whether to include all exposed roles or only selected ones, and save. Wait until the status shows the content was fetched successfully.
  4. In the Content Manager > Content Explorer, open the provider, select the roles and choose Add to My Content.
  5. Assign the roles to your site in the Site Settings.

Step 6: Assign both keys to the user

  • Key 1 (BTP): In the BTP cockpit under Security > Role Collections, assign ~s4h_SAP_BR_PURCHASER to Maria, or better, map it to an IdP group so assignments are managed centrally in your identity provider.
  • Key 2 (S/4HANA): Make sure Maria's SU01 user exists with the same identity used in the CERTRULE mapping, and assign SAP_BR_PURCHASER in PFCG/SU01.

Quick troubleshooting checklist

  • Tile is not visible: the BTP role collection is missing, the role is not assigned to the site, or the content was not re-fetched after a change in S/4HANA.
  • Tile is visible but the app fails with 401/403: check the Cloud Connector principal propagation setup, the CERTRULE mapping and the PFCG role assignment in S/4HANA.
  • Content provider fails to fetch: test the design-time destination and check that /sap/bc/ui2/cdm3/ is exposed in the Cloud Connector.

Conclusion

You cannot replace one key with the other. Federated BTP role collections exist for operational efficiency: they bring the launchpad layout from S/4HANA into Work Zone automatically, so you do not replicate catalogs and spaces by hand. PFCG roles exist for security: they enforce the data-level authorizations in the system of record. When a user reports "I can see the tile but the app doesn't work" (or the other way around), ask which of the two keys is missing, and you will usually find the answer quickly.

In upcoming posts, I will cover other Work Zone scenarios, including apps deployed on BTP, to complete the end-to-end picture.

entry.title: How SAP Build Work Zone Acts as Joule's Intent Solver: A Hands-On Walkthrough
entry.content:
Introduction

When a user asks Joule to "open Safety Manager", Joule doesn't decide on its own what that app is or whether the user may open it. SAP Build Work Zone's Navigation Service does that: it resolves the intent to a real, authorized launch target. In a recent project, I set this up end to end. We federated content from an on-premise SAP S/4HANA 2025 system into SAP Build Work Zone, standard edition, and I traced how a Joule request turns into an executable #SemanticObject-action intent.

What you will see, with screenshots from that work:

  • Exposing launchpad content from S/4HANA 2025 with Content Exposure v2
  • Design-time and runtime destinations through SAP Cloud Connector
  • The Content Channel settings that matter, and what to change at scale
  • Federated roles and the intents inside them, including why classic roles turn into #Shell-startGUI
  • The full path from a Joule prompt to a launched transaction

SAP's Joule setup guidance states it plainly: Joule uses the Navigation Service component of SAP Build Work Zone, standard edition, to resolve intent-based navigation targets. This post shows what that looks like in practice.

System IDs, host names and URLs in the screenshots are masked. Where an ID appears in the text, <SID> stands for the backend system ID.

The architecture in one picture

Joule understands the request, but Work Zone owns the answer to "which app, and is this user allowed?" Content reaches Work Zone through federation. The S/4HANA system exposes its roles, and Work Zone pulls them over a design-time destination through Cloud Connector.

The Navigation Service sits in the middle. If the role check fails, the intent is never returned to Joule, so the user never sees a launch card.

Step 1: Expose launchpad content from S/4HANA 2025

Work Zone can only resolve intents it knows about, so the first job is to publish the backend's roles and apps. Content federation reads them through the CDM3 service (/sap/bc/ui2/cdm3). CDM3 turns on-premise launchpad content into a standard JSON model that Work Zone understands.

On S/4HANA 2023 and 2025, exposure moved to Content Exposure version 2. In the backend I:

  1. Activated the HTTP services in SICF, including /UI2/FLP_CONTENT_EXPOSURE and the CDM3 endpoint.
  2. Allowed the services in UCON (UCON_HTTP_SERVICES / uconcockpit).
  3. Picked the roles to expose and ran the exposure (report /UI2/R_FLP_CONTENT_EXPOSURE).

Figure 1 – The content exposure HTTP service activated in SICF.

The exposure log is the proof point. It ended with "Content has been exposed and is ready to be picked up by SAP BTP."

Figure 2 – CDM3 exposure log. Roles and business apps are now available to BTP.

Tip: Activating the service only opens the door. Nothing reaches Work Zone until you actually choose the roles and run the exposure.

Step 2: Connect through Cloud Connector with two destinations

Work Zone needs two separate HTTP destinations in the BTP cockpit, both routed through SAP Cloud Connector. No backend port is exposed to the internet.

  Design-time destination Runtime destination

PurposeReads the content model (roles, catalogs, intents)Runs the apps when a user clicks or Joule launches
Used byChannel Manager, when fetching contentEnd users at runtime
AuthenticationTechnical userPrincipal propagation recommended

In Cloud Connector, I exposed /sap/bc/ui2/cdm3 with all sub-paths so the design-time destination could reach it. The runtime destination needs the additional properties that let Work Zone launch classic ABAP UIs:

Figure 3 – Runtime destination properties. sap-sysid must match the S/4HANA system ID and sap-client the target client.

What went wrong first: the initial URLs had extra path segments at the end. It worked once I removed the trailing entities from both destinations and set the runtime destination to protocol, host and port only.

Step 3: Create the Content Channel in Work Zone

In Work Zone's Channel Manager, I created a content provider that points to both destinations. This channel is what feeds the Navigation Service its intents.

Figure 4 – New content provider with the design-time and runtime destinations.

Setting What I used When to change it

Runtime destination for dynamic dataUse default runtime destinationMany live-count tiles: split that traffic onto its own destination
Content granularityRoles and related contentOlder NetWeaver or portal backends without Spaces and Pages
Automatically add all content itemsOnThousands of roles: turn it off and approve roles manually
Provision authorizations with IPSOff for the first rolloutRequired at scale, together with principal propagation
Include group and catalog assignmentsOff (S/4HANA 2025 uses Spaces and Pages)Older releases such as 1809 or 1909 that still rely on groups

After saving, the channel runs an update. Once it finishes, the backend's roles are in Work Zone.

Figure 5 – The new channel updating in Automatic Mode, next to the HTML5 Apps channel.

Step 4: Assign federated roles and inspect the intents

Federated roles arrive with a ~<SID>_ prefix, and the role is the unit of federation. Apps, catalogs and spaces sit inside their roles rather than as standalone objects. That's why Content Manager lists only roles at the top level.

Work Zone imported 59 roles and generated a matching BTP role collection for each one. Two assignments are needed before anything shows up:

  1. Assign the roles to the Work Zone site (Site Directory > Role Assignments).
  2. Assign the generated role collections to the user. Without this step, Work Zone hides the tiles even when the site has the role.

Figure 6 – Federated roles assigned to the Work Zone site.

Open any role in Content Manager and each app shows its navigation target. This is exactly what the Navigation Service hands back to Joule. A native Fiori app carries a real business intent:

Figure 7 – Role SAP_BR_ADMINISTRATOR_DANA: Customer Data Browser resolves to #CustomerDataPackage-preview (SAPUI5, Fiori ID F5746).

Why classic roles become #Shell-startGUI

This was the most interesting finding. The Safety Manager role (SAP_EHSM_HSS_SAFEMGR) came into Work Zone with just four apps, and none of them were business apps:

Figure 8 – Safety Manager role: the GUI launcher resolves to Shell-startGUI with parameter sap-ui2-tcode.

Checking the same role in the backend explained why. In the Launchpad Content Manager (/UI2/FLPCM_CUST), the role has zero tiles or target mappings:

Figure 9 – SAP_EHSM_HSS_SAFEMGR has no Fiori catalogs, so there are 0 target mappings.

The role is built from classic PFCG menu folders that contain SAP GUI transactions and Web Dynpro ABAP apps, not Fiori catalogs. The exposure engine can't give those their own semantic objects, so it wraps them in four generic launchers:

Work Zone app ID Inbound intent What it does

<SID>_businessapp.gui.generic#Shell-startGUIStarts any transaction in SAP GUI for HTML
<SID>_businessapp.wda.generic#Shell-startWDAStarts any Web Dynpro ABAP application
<SID>_businessapp.flp.search#Shell-searchEnterprise search on the backend
<SID>_businessapp.flp.homepage#Shell-homeReturns to the system's home page

What this means for Joule: for classic content, the intent Joule gets back is #Shell-startGUI plus a transaction code, not a business-specific intent. Authorization still applies, because the Navigation Service evaluates it against the federated Safety Manager role. A user without that role never gets the launcher.

End to end: from a Joule prompt to a running transaction

With this content in place, here is how a request like "Open Safety Manager GUI" moves through the stack. The numbers match the architecture diagram above.

  1. Prompt: the user types the request in the Joule chat.
  2. Intent extraction: Joule's language processing maps it to a target intent, #Shell-startGUI?sap-ui2-tcode=<TCODE>.
  3. Resolution in Work Zone: the Navigation Service checks the user's token (Global User ID and group claims from Cloud Identity Services). It verifies that the user has the federated Safety Manager role and, if so, returns the matching app descriptor.
  4. Navigation card: Joule shows a link to "Launch generic SAP GUI Application" with that target.
  5. Execution: the browser opens the transaction in SAP GUI for HTML on S/4HANA, through the runtime destination and Cloud Connector.

The key point is step 3. Joule contributes the language understanding, and Work Zone provides the catalog of valid, authorized targets. If the role isn't assigned, the Navigation Service drops the intent, and Joule has nothing to offer.

An earlier attempt ended here instead:

Figure 10 – A 403 when launching a Web Dynpro test app. The intent resolved, but the runtime call to the backend was refused.

Lessons learned

  • No federated role means no intent for Joule. When Joule "can't find" an app, check the user's role collections in BTP before touching Joule.
  • Expose, don't just activate. SICF and UCON only open the service. The exposure run is what publishes the roles.
  • Keep destination URLs clean. Leave trailing paths off. The runtime destination should be protocol, host and port only.
  • Open the CDM3 path in Cloud Connector, with all sub-paths, or the channel can't read content.
  • Know what your roles are made of. Classic PFCG roles give Joule generic #Shell-startGUI or #Shell-startWDA targets. Fiori-based business roles give specific intents such as #CustomerDataPackage-preview.
  • Plan for scale. Turn off auto-add for large systems, and turn on IPS provisioning with principal propagation.

Also worth knowing from SAP's Joule troubleshooting notes: if the Joule navigation button is missing, export the Navigation Service destination. Check that tokenServiceURLType is Dedicated, then refresh the content channel in Work Zone.

Wrapping up

Joule is the conversation layer, and SAP Build Work Zone's Navigation Service decides what a user can actually open. If you set up content federation carefully, Joule inherits your existing S/4HANA roles and apps as intents it can safely resolve.

Have you set up Joule with content federation from an on-premise system? I'd like to hear what you ran into, so share it in the comments.

entry.title: Natural Language (NL) Over SAP Data: A Practical MCP Pattern for Joule Desktop & Pro-Code Agent
entry.content:
Introduction

Any S/4HANA OData API, standard or custom, can be exposed as an MCP server through SAP Integration Suite's MCP Gateway and consumed by AI agents through two complementary paths: Joule Work Desktop for a direct, low-overhead experience, and a custom agent in Cloud Foundry that can be triggered in Joule SAP Build Work Zone for an orchestrated, reasoning-capable experience. 

To make it concrete, we applied it to SAP Production Revenue Accounting (PRA) data: a domain that is rich, complex, and mission-critical, and where the gap between the data and the people who need it is wide enough to make the pattern's value immediately visible. The solution is not PRA-specific. The same architecture applies to any standard or custom OData V4 service in S/4HANA: Finance, Plant Maintenance, Materials Management, Sales and Distribution, or any domain where business users need structured answers without writing queries or navigating transaction codes.

This blog walks through the architecture, the components, the implementation decisions, and the trade-offs behind the two access patterns we designed and deployed:

  1. Joule Work Desktop — connects directly to an custom MCP server published via SAP Integration Suite. Ideal for business users who want a direct AI interface to standard PRA revenue accounting tables.

  2. Joule in SAP Build Work Zone — routes through a custom AI agent on SAP Cloud Foundry that adds an intelligent reasoning layer. Ideal for business users already operating inside Work Zone.

Both patterns share the same backend: a custom OData V4 service exposing standard SAP PRA tables, published as an MCP server through SAP Integration Suite's MCP Gateway.

A full end-to-end walkthrough has been recorded as a companion to this blog.

Solution Architecture

The architecture is deliberately generic. Swap out the PRA OData service for any other S/4HANA OData V4 endpoint and the rest of the pattern holds unchanged.

The solution exposes standard S/4HANA PRA tables via a custom OData V4 service (built on ABAP RAP), publishes them as governed MCP tools through SAP Integration Suite's MCP Gateway, and surfaces them to business users via natural language either directly through Joule Work Desktop or through a custom AI agent embedded in SAP Build Work Zone.

Path 1 — Joule Desktop:

Desktop User → Joule Desktop → MCP → SAP Integration Suite → OData → S/4HANA

Path 2 — Joule in Work Zone:

Web User → SAP Build Work Zone (Joule) → A2A → Custom Agent on CF → MCP → SAP Integration Suite → OData → S/4HANA

Component Walkthrough

1. S/4HANA On-Premise — The Data Source

The data lives in a standard S/4HANA on-premise system. We exposed the standard PRA tables via a custom OData V4 service built using the ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model (RAP).

The service exposes all 13 entity sets with proper navigation associations, enabling deep $expand queries across both the Document and Revenue Distribution branches. 

 

2. SAP Integration Suite — MCP Gateway

This is the integration layer that bridges the RAP OData service into the AI world.

SAP Integration Suite's MCP Server capability (part of the MCP Gateway feature, available with the Premium subscription) consumes the OData V4 service metadata and automatically generates MCP tool definitions for every operation. For our 13-entity service, this produced 41 MCP tools covering list queries, filtered reads, and navigation operations.

Why MCP? The Model Context Protocol is an open standard for AI tool discovery and invocation. By publishing our OData service as an MCP server, we make it consumable by any MCP-compatible client, including Joule Work Desktop, LangChain agents, or any future client, without changing the backend.

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

The Developer Hub within Integration Suite is used to publish the MCP server, generating the OAuth credentials that clients use to authenticate. It also provides discoverability within the organization: other developers can find and reuse the same MCP server without rebuilding the integration from scratch.

3. SAP Cloud Foundry — Custom Reasoning Agent

For the Work Zone path, we built a custom Python agent deployed on SAP BTP Cloud Foundry. This agent adds the reasoning layer that bridges Joule's natural language input to structured MCP tool calls.

The agent stack:

ComponentRole

a2a-sdk

Implements the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol, exposing a JSON-RPC 2.0 endpoint that Joule can call

LangGraph + LangChain

ReAct (Reasoning + Acting) loop: decides which MCP tools to call, in what order, based on the user's question

langchain-mcp-adapters

Loads MCP tools from Integration Suite at runtime and wraps them as LangChain 

LiteLLM / langchain-litellm

Routes LLM calls to SAP AI Core using the standard OpenAI-compatible interface

The ReAct pattern is important here. Rather than a single-shot query, the agent reasons iteratively: it reads the question, identifies which MCP tools are relevant, calls them, evaluates the results, and decides whether additional calls are needed before formulating the final answer. This is what makes it capable of answering multi-hop questions that require joining data from multiple PRA tables.

4. Registering the A2A Agent with Joule

Deployment uses the Joule CLI. The deploy command registers the custom agent as a Joule capability. By default, this deploys to standalone Joule.

To surface the agent inside SAP Build Work Zone, update the assistant type to sap_digital_Assistant. The Joule Admin Center (accessible by appending /admin to the Joule instance URL) allows you to verify the deployment and confirm the capability is active.

5. SAP Build Work Zone - Registering the A2A Agent with Joule

SAP Build Work Zone is the standard business user entry point. Joule is embedded natively in the Work Zone shell,  no separate app to open, no separate login.

6. Joule Work Desktop Experience

For users who prefer the Joule Work Desktop standalone experience, the integration is simpler: Joule Work Desktop connects directly to the MCP server. No custom agent, no A2A, no Cloud Foundry deployment required.

Conclusion

The architecture supports two distinct experiences from the same foundation. Joule Work Desktop connects directly to the MCP server no agent required giving business users a fast, lightweight path to query SAP data in natural language. Joule in SAP Build Work Zone routes through a custom AI agent deployed on BTP Cloud Foundry, adding multi-step reasoning, tool orchestration, and a governed conversational interface for broader business user adoption.

The architecture is composable by design. The OData V4 service, MCP server, reasoning agent, and Joule capability are independent layers each doing one thing well. Swap the data source and the pattern applies to any SAP domain. Complexity lives where it belongs: the OData layer owns the data model, MCP handles tool discoverability, LangGraph handles reasoning, and Joule handles the conversation.

Consider which of your OData APIs could benefit from this pattern  a Finance posting service, a Plant Maintenance feed, a Sales Order status endpoint. Any of them can become a natural language interface using exactly this stack.
